summary: Defines a syntax for representing both GSTN (the global telephone network) addresses and Internet addresses in one place, for email services that mix the two such as fax over email. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2846 defines extra parts for e-mail addresses that represent telephone-network destinations. These parts can describe local dialing instructions, extensions, post-dial tones, and the intended recipient.

subtitle: A format for including telephone-network numbers and recipient details in e-mail addresses.

tldr.problem: The earlier minimal e-mail format for telephone-network addresses could not represent local dialing, subaddresses, post-dial sequences, or recipient details.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2846 extends the address syntax with local phone numbers, ISDN subaddresses, post-dial sequences, recipient names, and physical-delivery qualifiers.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 3191 and RFC 3192. New service selectors and qualifier values require IANA registration.

today: RFC 2846 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 3191 and RFC 3192. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Telephone Addresses Need More Detail
sections.content:
RFC 2846 extends the minimal syntax for representing Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN) addresses in e-mail. A phone number may need more information than a global number alone, such as a local dialing sequence or details that identify a recipient.

The syntax is written in Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF). Other specifications may add elements, but they must use the definitions in this RFC for elements it already defines.
sections.plainLanguage: A telephone destination may need local dialing instructions or an extension in addition to its number. This RFC defines a shared way to include those details in an e-mail address.

sections.title: Global and Local Phone Numbers
sections.content:
The gstn-phone form allows either a global phone number or a local phone number. A local number can include an exit code and a dial number, each made from phone-string characters such as digits, DTMF symbols, pauses, tone waits, and written separators.

The plus sign is reserved for global numbers and MUST NOT start a local-phone string. The meaning of pause and tone-wait characters depends on the destination mail transfer agent implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: A global number begins with a plus sign, while a local number can include dialing instructions for a particular telephone system. The characters for pauses and tone waits are interpreted by the destination mail system.

sections.title: Subaddresses and Post-Dial Sequences
sections.content:
An address can include an ISDN subaddress after /ISUB=. It can also include a post-dial sequence after /POSTD=, for additional dialing after the connection has been made, such as entering tones into an automated menu.

The ISDN separator and post-dial separator are case-insensitive. When a destination needs multiple subaddresses, e-mail uses a separate address element for each recipient; a user agent may accept multiple subaddresses but must generate multiple mailbox elements when submitting the message.
sections.plainLanguage: A subaddress can identify the final device or extension after the main number connects. A post-dial sequence can provide extra tones, such as selections in an automated menu.

sections.title: Names and Physical-Delivery Details
sections.content:
The optional pstn-recipient element can carry a recipient name using /ATTN=. It may also include qualifiers for details such as organization, office, street, postal address, post office box, postal code, or country.

Only the needed qualifiers SHOULD be included, because e-mail address length is limited by the applicable e-mail standards. The complete address must follow those standards' quoting rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The address can include a person's name and delivery details for a gateway to use, such as a street or office. Include only the details needed to identify the destination.

sections.title: Examples of Extended Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC's examples combine service selectors, phone numbers, subaddresses, post-dial sequences, and recipient names. For example, an address can put an ISDN subaddress after /ISUB= or a post-dial sequence after /POSTD=.

A complete e-mail address adds the gateway's domain after the local telephone-address portion. These examples illustrate the syntax and are not requirements for a particular dialing plan.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how the pieces fit together in an address. A service label and phone number can be followed by an extension, extra dialing instructions, and a gateway name.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
Because e-mail routing relies on DNS data, false or altered DNS information could redirect a message through a compromised mail gateway. The RFC also warns that private dialing codes included in local-phone strings may be visible to mail systems and may appear on fax cover pages.

RFC 2846 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 3191 and RFC 3192. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing data can be altered, and secret dialing codes in an address can be exposed while mail is handled. RFC 3191 and RFC 3192 later updated this Proposed Standard.
